parole.testo: Borrowed from Hungarian cirok, which in turn was borrowed from either from a Southern Slavic language (cf. Slovene sírek or Serbo-Croatian sirak), ultimately from Latin (granum) Syricum (“Syrian grain”).

Borrowed from Czech císař, from Proto-Slavic *cěsařь, *cěsarjь. Original form was ciesar (first attested in the 16th century; compare surnames Ciesar, Ciesarik) which was possibly borrowed from Gothic 𐌺𐌰𐌹𐍃𐌰𐍂 (kaisar). First attested in the 13th century.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *jьstъba. From either Old High German stuba or a Romance word (compare French étuve).
Cognate with or from Lithuanian gintaras, possibly via Russian янтарь (jantarʹ). Compare also Latvian dzintars.

Inherited from Old Slovak pohár, derived from Hungarian pohár, from Old High German pehhari, from Late Latin bicarium, possibly from bacarium, or from Ancient Greek βῖκος (bîkos). Cognate with Pannonian Rusyn погар (pohar).

Inherited from Old Slovak svatba, from Proto-Slavic *svatьba. Compare Old Church Slavonic сватьба (svatĭba), which is normally derived from Proto-Slavic *svatiti sę (a verb in meaning of "to become a relative"). Compare Slovak svatať (a dialectal verb for "someone to woo into marriage, to get engage

parole.significato: telescope (a monocular optical instrument that magnifies distant objects, especially in astronomy)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin tēlescopium, or borrowed from Italian telescòpio; both from Ancient Greek τηλεσκόπος (tēleskópos, “far-seeing”). By surface analysis, tele- (“tele-”) + -skop (“-scope”). First attested in the 19th century.
Possibly borrowed from German Tiger, or a learned borrowing from Latin tigris; from Ancient Greek τῐ́γρῐς (tĭ́grĭs), probably of Iranian origin. First attested in the 17th century.
